What I want to understand from you when you say they wore police insignia, you mean insignia of police units attached to the public security department of the MUP?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those are the insignia worn by the police. There is no crucial difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know when the Wolves went into Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the Drina Wolves?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already answered that question. This was approximately when the Skorpions appeared there, too, this was sometime in April, perhaps a couple of days before or after, but more or less at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When were the crimes that you spoke of committed at Podujevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The crime in Podujevo was committed on the 31st of March, 1999, when the first -- when Slobodan Medic, Boca, and the Skorpions were in Kosovo for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So if the Drina Wolves went to Kosovo when the Skorpions appeared there, they would have gone to Kosovo at approximately the end of March?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Skorpions were there for the first time and they committed the crime on the 31st of March, and then they were returned. Mr. Ivetic put that question, they were returned to Prolom Banja in April. They went back again, and sometime between the 10th and the 15th of May they were brought back from Kosovo again; and according to our information, they did not go back to Kosovo again. The second time thus they went to Kosovo, it's possible that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The problem arises I think because you are not answering the questions asked. I'm just asking you when the Drina Wolves went to Kosovo, and you told me that they appeared at the same time as the Skorpions, and we know that the Skorpions went there two times. And that is why we are spending a long time on a very small issue. Can you tell me when, in which month, the Drina Wolves appeared in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: April.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know who -- under whose authority they were brought there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know when they left Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know if they were there for the duration of the war?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in April 1999 they were there. For how long, though, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know what they were doing in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have concrete information that they committed any crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know what they were doing in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have any information. We just registered that they were in Kosovo, but as for exactly what they did, that they were in Kosovo Polje and in private houses, so on, but we didn't have specific information as to what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I noted here, General, that you said in respect to these groups --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The microphone is turned off.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: -- That you had sources among them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So didn't your sources among them tell you what the Drina Wolves were doing in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information that was there came more from sources from Republika Srpska from those who monitored it and let us know or alerted us that they had come to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, just tell me - and you know as His Honour indicated, you can say you don't know if you don't know - did your sources within this group tell you what they were about in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, I have it in my mind that we've heard evidence that there were instructions issued by VJ command that there should not be paramilitaries operating at all. Was that your understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was specified, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On what basis then would it be appropriate to ignore the presence of the Wolves from Drina in Kosovo, as you appear to have done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because the order that came from the Supreme Command Staff was not respected; the army respected it, but the MUP did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You weren't concerned about this at the end of March then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And in spite of that, you were unable to establish anything at all about the activities of the Wolves in the Drina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We tried, but during that time we could not gather relevant or specific data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: They sound more like foxes than wolves. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Arkan group, on whose authority did they go to Kosovo, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the state security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who in the state security department?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The department chief, Mr. Rade Markovic, the RDB chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: They were -- they went down there and they wore SAJ uniforms, uniforms of the public security department. Did he authorise that they were to be attached to units of the public security department?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if he authorised them, but all I know is that Arkan offered 100 men for Kosovo and that Rade Markovic suggested that he report to the army and that they be included or that they join the military as volunteers. And then 30 of his men were taken and sent to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So these 30 men were sent to Kosovo and went to Kosovo as volunteers of the army?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not volunteers of the army, but through the RDB. Markovic suggested to Arkan to join the ranks of the army. He categorically refused that, and then he was sent by the RDB, 30 of his men, that is. That is to say they had nothing to do army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So I'll ask you this again in respect to Arkan's men. What did your sources among them tell you they were doing in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our sources registered their presence in the territory of Kosovo Polje. We did not have anything more specific up until the very eve of the meeting held at Milosevic's on the 17th of May; namely, that some members - we didn't know who - committed a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Maybe it's my misunderstanding, because I noted that you said that we had sources among them, which you said. What do you mean when you say that, We had sources among them, including the Arkan group?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said that among Boca's men we had sources; as for Arkan's, well we had some contacts but not quality sources. However, we found out when they were in the territory of Kosovo, we found out through some other sources that they had committed a crime, that they killed two persons, and that was later confirmed by Rade Markovic as being correct, and that they were arrested and under investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you don't know whether or not they took part in any operations by the security forces while they were in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as soon as they got there -- I mean, they came on account of some activity. They did not come just to sit around. Whoever came to Kosovo came for some activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you tell us that you don't know what they were doing down there. You tell us that they came there for some activity. So I'm asking if you know whether or not they were involved in any operations by the security forces in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not participate on the part of the army. As for the MUP side, or rather, in terms of the tasks of the RDB, I don't know. I don't know exactly. I don't know specifically, but I know that they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Pauk, when did Pauk become -- or when did Pauk attend in Kosovo as members of the 125th Motorised Brigade? Just give me a month and a -- a date and a month, if you can.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: April, around the 20th or right after the 20th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When did the army - when I say "the army," I mean you in the command of the army, the Supreme Command - discover that they were not -- or did not fulfil the regular procedure to join the army?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sometime in the beginning of May, because after that I was at that reception centre called Grocka near Belgrade in order to carry out an inspection of that reception centre. Then this information that we had were confirmed; that is to say, the security organs who were there confirmed our suspicions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So when were they -- well, removed from the army?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were removed sometime around mid-May, and Petrusic and Orasanin and I think two other members were brought into Belgrade to be interviewed by us, and the interview started on the 18th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So were they arrested or were they taken into custody -- well, were they arrested and charged for anything or were they released?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were brought in for an interview. They were taken into custody. Interviews with them were held for about a week I think. After that they were handed over to the State Security Service because we did not have any proof of their espionage activities, and also there was no evidence of them having committed a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the timing of this now being linked to the meeting on the 17th of May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're right, Mr. Bonomy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So were they taken to Belgrade for interview only after that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, on the 18th of May, that's when the interview started. On the 17th, that gathering was informed, the gathering chaired by then-President Milosevic, and he said then that the situation should be cleared up with them. And we were supposed to do this together with the State Security Service; however, they obstructed that, so we resolved the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So what became of them, did they -- were they released and did they remain in the country?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were handed over to the State Security Service because there was no proof in order to have criminal charges brought against them. But since the State Security Service had discovered that they were planning some unlawful activity, including some threats of assassinations, they were arrested, and they were in detention, or rather, in prison until the political changes took place in Serbia on the 5th of October, 2000, when they were amnestied.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's discuss briefly, if we may, the Serbian Liberation Army. You were shown Exhibit 593 and we -- I don't think we need to go into it, which referred to the Serbian Liberation Army. Was that a group that was attached to the MUP or to the VJ?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not attached to anybody. This was a group in the territory of Krusevac that had been formed by Lieutenant Gajic, who has the same last name as I do, and it involved a number of civilians. This group collected weapons and they planned to go to Kosovo. There were even some threats issued there in -- among other things, they threatened to assassinate Nebojsa Pavkovic, commander of the 3rd Army. The service discovered that, followed that, documented it, arrested them. They were taken to court, a trial was held, and they were all convicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I want to ask you about. The service arrested them for what? What were they charged for?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were charged for illegal organisation and arming with a view to going to Kosovo as a separate paramilitary formation outside the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Which service charged them?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The counter-intelligence service, we who were in charge of the entire action.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is the counter-intelligence service of the 1st, 2nd, 3rd Army, or of the General Staff, or of a particular brigade?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the 3rd Army, although when this matter was being dealt with, the matter of that group, there was General Aleksandar Vasiljevic, who was there in charge of the entire action from the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, that really is my next question. Where were they charged? And I don't mean if you can relate when to an event. If you can tell when in terms of a month and a date?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's going to be hard for me to remember that. I know that it was during the war. Now, was it second, or rather, was it February or March 1999? So -- no, no, not February or March. It could have been April or May, during the course of the war, April or May 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Were they charged in a military court or in a civilian court?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In a military court, because the leader of that group was a lieutenant of the Army of Yugoslavia, Lieutenant Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, did you in respect to the groups in Kosovo, the Drina Wolves, the Arkan group, investigate -- well, not the Drina Wolves, the Arkan's group, let's ask about that one. Did you investigate and submit any reports on any or on the crime that you knew they were accused of?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because this was the jurisdiction of the civilian court. That was supposed to be taken up by the civilian judiciary, and Mr. Markovic said that investigation was under way against these individuals, these men of Arkans who had killed those two old Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like to move on to something else. You were shown quite a few documents which you said were briefing notes of the meetings of the Supreme Command. Just a couple questions about them, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we have a look at one of them, 3D606. If we could just focus on the B/C/S copy of it, the first page. There are only three pages or four pages on this one. And go to the last page, the last page in B/C/S, just B/C/S we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What I wanted to ask you is: How were these documents, do you know how this particular document was created?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see any document. From the briefing I only have -- oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It looks to see as though it's a computer print-out and it is unsigned.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, these are minutes from the briefing held at the Supreme Command Staff that was done every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who prepared these records?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were prepared by the chef de cabinet to the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command. Every evening there was a briefing and he made brief notes, and then this was compiled.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you review them at all in 1999 after they were compiled?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only when I was called as a witness; that is when this was made available to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about two or three months ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You noticed that a document -- these briefing notes that are shown, they appear with no stamp, they are not signed, and they bear no writing. Do you know whether or not these are -- were produced as computer print-outs?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. This is an abbreviated version that was compiled at every briefing, then it would be printed out. As for all briefings at the Supreme Command Staff, they were all recorded, taped and there is an extensive version of the remarks of all members of the Supreme Command Staff. This is just an abbreviated version, because at the end the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command would conclude the briefing and issue specific assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, where are the tapes of these -- of the briefing themselves? Do you know where they are kept?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably they should be in the archives of the army. I don't know now because something was changed in view of changes in the set-up of the army, but they must be in the archives.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, do you know - and either you do or you don't - whether or not this document was abbreviated or could have been abbreviated at a time when preparations were made to print it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As it was written, important points as they were jotted down, that's how it was printed out afterwards. I don't think it was necessary to abbreviate that because after that the assignments issued by the Chief of Staff of the Supreme Command followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were shown also documents purporting to be reports from the security organs of the Pristina Corps and the 3rd Army. How were those reports made, do you know?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is to say that there were several methods. One were the telegrams that arrived in the security administration, and another method were the reports that were formalised and that had to have a certain format; and there were regulations to that effect, what the format should be and what the content should include.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, let's look at one of them. Let's look at 10 -- 3D1033. Most of them bear the format that you see there, General. Is that a typewritten report, a telegram? What format is this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a telegram.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you see some writing to the top right-hand corner? Whose writing is that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was written when it arrived in the security administration. Then, this is -- well, I mean, this is handed over to the operatives and to the analysis people, and there are initials there. And I cannot decode that now. They jot down notes or a task that should be carried out in relation to that telegram and who was supposed to carry out that task, and then it's signed by initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I take it you were also shown these in preparation for your testimony here. Before you were shown them in preparation for testimony, when had -- when had you seen them before, if you had seen them before?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not necessarily for me to have a look at them beforehand. All these telegrams went through my hands. I was assistant for counter-intelligence and at the same time deputy head of department in the security administration. So they all went through my hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, the intelligence that is -- or the information that you have recorded in the reports from the security organs that you spoke about in court, they -- it comes from a variety of sources. In answer to a question by Mr. Ivetic, you said that you could not tell the source. When you say you could not tell the source, is it because you don't know these sources personally or is it because you would not for any other reason, perhaps security?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for this question. In all services of the world, including our own as well, there are several categories of sources. There are some sources that are registered and have a code, which means that there is a legal regulation or obligation on the part of the state that if something happens to them, they should be entitled to social security, medical treatment, and so on, so that's a secret. They can be disclosed, but only through a special order. Then there are other operative sources that are a lower category who, unless the sources ask to be protected, can be disclosed. But the first category, the registered ones, they enjoy full protection because the consequences can be grave if their identity is disclosed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I was just asking you, when you told Mr. Ivetic that you could not tell him your sources, was that because you did not know who the source was or was there another reason? Was it because you would not do it for another reason?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, I, quite simply, don't know. Who could remember all of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I'd have to check that. So there was no other reason but that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Among the sources that you received information from in 1999 was the security service of the MUP, they were one of the sources?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was the RDB, because by virtue of our powers and tasks, we mostly coordinate with the RDB, less with the MUP. It's the military police that cooperates with the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the RDB, I take it, also was one of the sources for information to the Pristina Corps security organ and the 3rd Army security organ?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and they often exchanged information because this is within the authority of the RDB, to cover a territory and to have their sources in all structures. That is their main task.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And some of the documents you spoke about referred to information from sources abroad, in Switzerland and even Albania. Were these sources that were attached to the security organ or they were sources of the RDB or they were sources of military intelligence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Combined sources, both RDB and the military counter-intelligence service and also some information and data came from the military intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who conducted the electronic surveillance that some of these documents refer to? What was the source of it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Electronic surveillance centres that were run by the military that had the appropriate equipment and some of the data that the counter-intelligence service was interested in, we got that regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Wouldn't you agree with me that you relied upon sources, for example, the RJB, for information which you used but you subsequently developed that -- you subsequently realised that the information you got from the sources was incorrect?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't fully agree with your conclusion. First of all, the data that we got were either fully verified or verified to a high degree. And even the data that we got from the other sources, the state security and so on, we would verify them. And the developments later on proved that those data were, indeed, accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, your chief of the security department for the Pristina Corps was Momir Stojanovic; that's correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The head of the security sector; the security department is at the army level.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, the department that was providing these reports that you spoke of, he was one of the persons who was providing these reports, the security organ of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but with regard to Kosovo all other security organs of the Army of Yugoslavia were under an obligation to provide reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know that Mr. Stojanovic in 2003 in an interview said that a lot of the reports that were submitted to the army by the state security turned out to be incorrect and that in many cases the army acted on the information, employed significant forces, but it was almost always shown that this was not necessary. Do you recall whether or not he said that in an interview?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember that interview, but he meant the data related primarily to the strength of the terrorist forces. Because those were the data that the military had, and we, the military counter-intelligence service, that came -- and also the data that came from the RDB were diametrically opposed. I think that they actually overestimated the number of terrorists. It was way higher in their estimate than it actually was. I think that our data were, in fact, more reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, the interview I'm speaking of -- in that interview you are speaking of the flow of the weapons across the border. But the point I want to make is this, and I should correct myself, that interview was conducted in the year 2000 when you were still, I believe, employed to the security -- the state security department. And I take it if your subordinate made a statement like that, you would be aware of it. And the statement is that you received information from state security, intelligence from state security, which you acted upon, that is, you believed it to be true; and that was the basis of policy and operations by the army. And later on it turned out to be false. Did you know that he said that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that he said that because at that time he was not in the military security service. After the -- after graduating from the war school, I think immediately after that, he took up a command post as a brigade commander. So he was not in the security service. He was not a security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know that General Lazarevic after the war, the same year, December 2000, also said the same thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've let this go long enough but I think I should be objecting. Mr. Stamp for the last several questions has been using a document for which he listed for cross-examination for which we have an objection and I think he knows we have an objection to it and I think he's asking these questions in a way to get around that objection, but he's misphrasing the fact that this is an interview. What Mr. Stamp is using is a -- is a news journal article from a weekly tabloid, it's even identified as a tabloid, and it is an English translation, summary, prepared by FBIS, which I think we've had discussions previously as being affiliated with the state department or the CIA and then there's the B/C/S translation of the English translation. So we don't even have the original text of this article that purports to have been taken. And to keep calling it an interview and saying persons said X, Y, and Z is far from the truth. This is not a sworn statement, this is a tabloid. I think we all know what that means. I think Mr. Stamp by not addressing this point is creating a false impression with his questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I asked the question whether he knew something had been said; if he knows it he knows it, if he does not know it, he does not. But I'm surprised because I thought that counsel was saying in the course of his cross-examination the same point I'm trying to get to, that perhaps these reports are not necessarily reliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The objection is to you characterising the material that you're using as an interview, and as if you had word for word the statement that were made. I don't think the objection is to you asking whether the witness knew the sort of information that you're gleaning from the document. Because if he doesn't, it comes to nothing; and if it does, well, it's his evidence, it's nothing to do with the document itself. So subject to that, you can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The report of the interview I have here, General, is that General Lazarevic said after the war --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have to support Mr. Ivetic's word and just give you one example. In this report that Mr. Stamp is trying to quote, it is stated that General Lazarevic is the Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia and the 3rd Army or some other unit is mentioned under the name of the 3rd Military District. I think this is quite sufficient for you to be able to determine the relevance of this source for the asking of questions. I think that we could analyse it and find a host of such examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not putting the source, I'm not addressing the source --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why do you bother then saying: "The report of the interview I have here is that General Lazarevic said after the war ..."?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I wish him to comment on what General Lazarevic is reported to have said; if he knows it, he knows it, if he does not, he does not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What you've heard already from Mr. Visnjic is good reason to question the accuracy of this. Why don't you just ask him the straight question, whether X, whichever it is from the report, is his understanding of the position. Otherwise, you're going to create anxiety among Defence counsel and constantly be interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know, General, that in 1999 the security organs received information primarily from the SDB, acted on the information in the belief that the information was true, and subsequently discovered that the information was not true?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this question would call for a more complex answer. Many pieces of information came in with varying degrees of being verified. Some were completely unverified, some were fully verified. The security organs, their reports mostly contained information that had been verified, had been accurate. And further developments confirmed that that was in case. But they also provided information that was not correct, but they thought they were indicative of something and they thought the security administration had to know that. We in the security administration approached these data very carefully, and we reported to the state and military leadership only on those things that were verified. If anything was unverified, we indicated that by saying, This is raw operative intelligence, hasn't been verified. That's what we indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. But what I wanted to know - and I'll just give you a specific example --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please try to answer the question you're being asked, Mr. Gajic. What you did was not answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I will repeat it and this time particularise. Did the security department or security administration receive information in respect to weapons crossing the border for the KLA from the state security sector and this information was acted upon because you believed it, you deployed -- you caused the army to deploy resources on the basis of this information, but later on you discovered the information was false?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Before the witness answers I would like to ask you, I know that I may be wasting your time, but I don't want to be accused of dealing with this matter in front of the witness. I would like to ask for the witness to step out of the courtroom. You agreed with our objections, you agreed that this document was not valid, but Mr. Stamp on the basis of this document, the purported interview, created a base misleading the witness into believing that somebody may have said something. But what is stated in the interview is the complete opposite, and if you allow me I will read it out in front of the witness what is stated in this purported interview. It is the exact opposite to what Mr. Stamp is asking about, and he made this foundation that this was based on this purported interview --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just give us a moment to consider the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. We don't agree that there is anything inappropriate in the question that has just been asked, and we require the witness to answer that question. Mr. Stamp, if you wish to put it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did the security service receive information about the movements of weapons across the border by the KLA, and on the basis of this information cause the army or gave information to the army and the army deployed on the basis of this information, yet later on it was discovered that this information was false?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would phrase it in a different way, but I will answer your question. The information was not inaccurate, but those who wanted to cross illegally with the weapons from the territory of Albania either changed their minds or decided that they couldn't go through or they had some information from their own sources that the military setting up the ambush and gave up on the intention, and then tried some ten days later on a different location. But there was some information, of course, that wasn't quite reliable, but if we're talking about weapons smuggling across the border, that was a rare occurrence, if I recall it correctly. I'm -- I apologise, Mr. Prosecutor, but the KLA had their own intelligence service, too, and they monitored every movement of the army. They had it active in Albania and in Kosovo, and they had air support in order to be able to monitor everything that was going on at the state border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did I accurately note your answer there as being to the effect that weapons smuggling across the border was a rare occurrence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, quite the contrary. This was quite intense, and I spoke about it, how it developed in stages. And I said - let me remind you, sir - that in July and August 1998 alone there were 72 border incidents at the border with Albania in the Pristina Corps area. 196 in 1998 as a whole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is a translation issue. I'm just trying to find out what your answer was. You said: "But if we're talking about weapons smuggling across the border, that was," something, "if I recall it correctly." Now, what was it you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said in answer to Mr. Prosecutor's question about the reliability of the information, I said that for the most part this information was reliable --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have that. It's not that point I'm asking you about. We've got your answer on that. You said something about how regularly weapons were smuggled across the border. Now, what did you say about that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Rare occurrence refers to the unreliability.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were such attempts every day, more successful or less successful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, and I now understand it that the reference to rare occurrence was to the occasions when the information was inaccurate. It's my misunderstanding of the position. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were shown documents, 3D1033, 3D1035, and 3D1052. I think -- well, these documents relate to the events that took place in Podujevo just before -- well, in the latter part of December 1998. And basically, these documents reflect - and I don't think I need to go into the details - these documents indicate that a combat group of the 15th Armoured Brigade were engaged in exercises in Pristina [sic] and they were fired upon by the KLA, and that is how they became embroiled in an action against the KLA. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that the wording of the question is incorrect. I don't think it's Pristina, but if the witness knows what this is all about. It should be Podujevo, but apparently the witness understood what it was all about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Podujevo, I understood what this was in reference to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: My apologies, and thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you look at 3D -- sorry, P928, and having regard to the information that you had, I would like you to comment on what I'm about to show you. And it's page 14 in English of P928, and that is page 15 in the B/C/S copy. This is General Dimitrijevic speaking if we look at the previous page, we realise that General Dimitrijevic was head of the MUP is speaking. And he says: "In addition, the current situation in the vicinity of Podujevo, I think that we must be completely consistent here and completely open towards each other" --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, before this gets too far out, I don't believe General Dimitrijevic was head of the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I keep making errors, I'm sorry. I meant head of security administration of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And since there's an interruption I might add that this was the 30th of December, 1998, shortly after those reports that you had from the Pristina Corps security organ were written. He's saying in respect to these events: "I think that we must be completely consistent here and completely open towards each other, so to speak. This situation in Podujevo and the surroundings, it was complex before, but when did it suddenly become even more complicated. After the so-called pretend or real planned exercises in which this company took part in the field. General, these sorts of moves will lead us to disaster. The explanation that this was a planned exercise, that is not true. It was planned that the unit would provoke the terrorists so that the MUP would then have to do whatever it had to do." You will agree with me that what the general, General Dimitrijevic, here is telling General Ojdanic is not consistent with what was in these reports.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to the report of the security section of the Pristina Corps dated the 19th of December, right at the bottom of this report it says that the combat group of the 15th Armoured Brigade went out to conduct training at Batlavsko Jezero where it had its training area, then that would be it. There is a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The difference is that the reports, in particular 1035, were that the groups were engaged in legitimate training exercises, whereas General Dimitrijevic is telling the Chief of Staff that they were not. It was a pretend exercise. So you agree that it's inconsistent to this extent?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Dimitrijevic's intervention is quite inconsistent. I can't quite really understand it. He does not believe in what his subordinate is reporting, the chief of section. He says that he has other information. He's not asking the chief of the sector to send a detailed report to him about what had really happened, and if there are any problems or any doubtful parts, he has to speak the truth. He does not tell the Chief of General Staff the foundation for such claims, but simply presents the problems. If I had been in his shoes, if I had presented these data, I would have said fair and square what the data were. I would ask the Chief of General Staff to set up a team, first of all. I would ask the sector chief to send a detailed report, and then I would require that a team be dispatched down to the field and to check what the situation really was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it is, in my opinion, these are just empty words.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well -- but you would agree with me that General Dimitrijevic found the report -- the reports in respect to Podujevo, and three of them we have, to be unreliable. He did not rely upon them in his personal report to the Chief of General Staff.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's the chief of the security administration, and if he goes to the Chief of General Staff he had to have the accurate information and he has to say where he got the different data from. He cannot simply present a problem without explaining what it is all about, because the Chief of the General Staff cannot make any decision based on this. The security administration is there precisely ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Incidentally -- before I move on -- well, I think the point is obvious --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder, Mr. Gajic, if you're putting the onus on the right person here. What Dimitrijevic is saying is that he doesn't accept that this was a planned exercise, and nobody disagrees with him do they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not agree with you. In the conclusion, General Ojdanic asserts that it was confirmed through the 3rd Army command and that it is an exercise. This is in the conclusion of the collegium session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that on a later page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I believe it's towards the end or at the very end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we see that page, Mr. Stamp, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry. The conclusions begin on page 21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But I'm not -- the witness would need to point to precisely what he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, indeed. So can we go to page 21, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not sure what page that is in the B/C/S copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, can you give us the references?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I check, I think they said that it was page 17, towards the end of the B/C/S version, and it's page 18 in e-court, at the bottom of the page, and I'm still looking. Page 17 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, can you help me, Mr. Gajic, to identify what's said to contradict Dimitrijevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a lot of discussion on other topics as well, and it went back and forth, but there is a part where General Ojdanic talks about how through the 3rd Army command this was checked. And in essence, the unit really was in exercises.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have hard copy for witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, I can see it --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- For myself at the moment, I'm reading it on the page. Well, we can interpret that in due course in the light of all the evidence. Please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, I would suggest to the witness that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General Ojdanic does not say that it was investigated and a conclusion contrary to what General Dimitrijevic had said was the result.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You -- Mr. Visnjic, is there still a problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the question is not clear to me. Is Mr. Stamp reading or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on, he's entitled to lead and you can re-examine on this. It's for Mr. Stamp to deal with this how he thinks appropriate. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You had told us that notwithstanding what General Dimitrijevic said, that General -- that General Ojdanic asserted in the conclusion that it was confirmed to the 3rd Army command that it is an exercise. Well, firstly, I suggest to you that General Ojdanic did not say so, that was confirmed that it was an exercise. Do you agree with that or do you disagree?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you permit me I would like to read the first and the second sentence, please. General Ojdanic states here: It is claimed that the situation at Podujevo was additionally caused by the presence of this unit, which is really just a question of whether the marching direction is correct and the place of its location picked for that, but really it was out in the camp. This is something that I was convinced of by the army commander. However, General Perisic at the time, when he withdrew the conditions of withdrawal. So I do not know why General Dimitrijevic did not ask the same thing from the security person of the Pristina Corps. For sure he had the correct information and had his own information that he received from the security administration, and then the whole truth or the real truth should have been stated. And if anyone had made a mistake, that person should have been called to account. This is what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well -- and you might well correct on what you think, but you will agree with me that the general, the person in charge of the security administration, was not relying on at least three security administration reportings in respect to this matter. He relied on what you just described here as his own information. You will agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say that that was his own information. He had another source.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Had it been his own information, he would have said that that was his assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In respect to President -- withdrawn. In respect to General Dimitrijevic, you said that he had options when he was removed, he was offered a position in the Ministry of Defence. Did he take up that position?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was General Perisic offered the same position and also refused to take it up?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Perisic was offered a position in the federal government, whereas General Dimitrijevic, you're right, was offered a position in the federal Ministry For Defence, the position of the coordinator of the work of the counter-intelligence and the military intelligence service, and he refused that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know if it's a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is convenient, Mr. Stamp, yes. We have to break again, Mr. Gajic. It will again be for 20 minutes, so we will be starting again at five minutes past 6.00. Could you leave the courtroom, please, with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I should make it clear before we rise that when we return we will be without Judge Chowhan, who has an important personal matter to deal with. And we've decided that in the circumstances we should continue in the interests of justice; and therefore, we will resume at five past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In paragraph 15 of your statement you spoke about the results of the counter-intelligence -- counter-terrorist operation in Kosovo which you said commenced -- commenced in July. And you said that the security administration department monitored these operations. And during the course of your testimony, probably most of your testimony, you spoke about your reports from the security organs, indicating that during the period of this counter-terrorist offensive evacuations or movement of Kosovar Albanians was caused by actions from the KLA. We have before the Court figures that were published by the UN human -- the United Nations High Commission for Refugees, which show that during the time approximating to when this offensive was going on, from say June to October, the 4th of October, 1998, the amount of displaced persons from Kosovo moved from 57.000 in June to 280.000 in October. Now, what I want to ask you is this: Is it your evidence that this displacement was caused exclusively by the KLA evacuating people?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't the only reason. There was several reasons, when we're talking about the KLA. So, no, not just that. There were several reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was one of the reasons the use of indiscriminate and excessive force by Serbian security forces?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what is meant by excessive use of force.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may -- if I may reply. I'm sorry if I seemed impolite, but perhaps I can respond. In Kosovo regarding the tactics of the KLA, it was the practice, quite frequent practice, to fortify houses, settlements, entire villages and to arm them. Previously the population would be moved out or they would stay, and they would open fire at whoever passed. If it was an open road there would be firing at the security forces, civilians, et cetera. And now if the problem was being resolved with such a terrorist force's stronghold, then let's say houses would be destroyed. I don't know if that is excessive use of force. Excessive use of force, in my view, would be if a village was entered and destroyed without any reason or cause. I don't know if I was -- if I managed to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, do you know of any -- of instances where Yugoslav forces committed crimes against Kosovar Albanian civilians during the course of this anti-terrorist offensive?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, and that is why I and General Vasiljevic went to Kosovo in June because there was such criminal instances already, and when we were investigating this problem of the crimes we learned that there were such cases and investigations were launched, they were processed, some were not processed, and so on and so forth. So the answer is: Yes, there were such cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Prosecutor can specify the time-frame that the question relates to, because there's obviously been a misunderstanding between him and the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said "June." I was speaking about 1998, the counter-terrorist offensive in 1998 that you spoke of in your statement. Do you know of the VJ, for example, shelling villages that were populated by civilians?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have such information nor did we have information about crimes in the course of 1998, in the course of this anti-terrorist operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know that the VJ shelled villages in 1998?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I responded more or less. Perhaps there were such instances of, as you say, shelling, but it's a question of which circumstances prevailed, if it was just purely shelling for the purposes of destruction. There were the anti-terrorist forces then, that meant the terrorist forces were being destroyed. I mean, I don't know, perhaps. I can't really speak about it off the top of my head now, but I do believe that this distinction needs to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: During the period of that offensive, did your security organs report to you that a variety of diplomats and representatives from the countries of the Contact Group were visiting Kosovo to observe the conditions that obtained there in respect to the offensive?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is yes, but we had information not only from the counter-intelligence organs from Kosovo. We also had information because we had regular legal contacts with the military and diplomatic representatives of the foreign countries accredited in Belgrade, and we knew that they went to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. Now, did your security service or the VJ at any time disclose to these visiting diplomats the information in respect to the evacuation of the Kosovar Albanians from these villages?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because that was not strictly our sphere. There was a special separate administration liaison with foreign military and diplomatic representatives. We did not have contacts of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But all of the Contact Group countries had military attaches, didn't they? For example, there was Colonel Crosland from the British side. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I told you military diplomatic representatives, I was thinking about the military attaches, yes. I know Mr. Crosland; he was the British military attache.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And he was one among many -- one among many who conducted tours of these areas with various visiting dignitaries. Did your liaison with the military attaches disclose to them the information that you were receiving in these reports about the movement of Kosovar Albanians at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did -- later on when the KVM was there after October, did you disclose to any of the KVM -- any member of the KVM leadership the information in these reports that KVM personnel were involved in assisting the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a Federal Commission, which I think was entrusted with the implementation of the agreement, if that's what you're thinking from October 1998, and the Federal Commission included not -- I mean had not just our information but other information too. And probably in these contacts, this is my assumption so I don't know, probably they did announce certain things and exchange some information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, this is not some information. I'm speaking about specific information now. You are saying that you were engaged in a counter-terrorist operation or a counter-terrorist conflict in that period, and you are saying that members of the KVM were involved in assisting people that you labelled terrorists. Did you make any official complaint to the KVM or any international body in respect to the individuals that you were getting these reports from who were involved in assisting the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, I didn't quite understand your question. Yes, we reported the state and the military leadership. We passed on information, the regular information that we had. There was a list of users who also received this information of ours, and the information, amongst other things, dealt with the matters that you asked me about, although the bulk of the verification mission were honourable and they were performing their duties correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What are the names of the individuals you reported were involved according to these security organ reports that are exhibited?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to give the example of the chief of mission, Mr. Walker, but it wasn't only our reports. Also reports of other specialised agencies, including the military intelligence agency, and you probably know that there were even some requests to have him dismissed from that position of head of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Mr. Walker was the head of the mission. I'm talking about the KVM personalities or the KVM staff on the ground. Did you report any of them by name for collaboration with the --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part they were correct, fair, but often a number of them - I don't want to generalise - would go beyond the framework provided by the agreement as far as control of the military was concerned, and also when they were in contact with people from the KLA they were inclined towards them in the sense of tolerating their acts of terrorism and violations of the agreement. Because it is known that the leadership of the KLA never recognised the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, that is not directly -- I'd like to move on. Can you answer me yes, no, I don't know. Do you know of a report being made naming any member of the KVM, apart from the head, of collaborating with the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such reports, but I could not give you the names now. I could not recall, but there were such reports. I do not remember specific names.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: To whom were these reports made?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, through regular reporting channels; that is to say, towards the General Staff and the state leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That's not what I'm asking you, General. Your evidence is that this international organisation, the OSCE, came into Kosovo to perform a monitoring procedure and that some persons within this organisation were engaged in collaborating with people you call terrorists. Did you make official reports in respect to these people to the OSCE itself or to any international body?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we could not because the security administration has its superiors; that is to say that it cannot directly send reports to the OSCE. It has to observe the chain of reporting, and we sent this to our superiors. As to what they did with that is -- that's not the affair of the security administration. It's for us to send the information we have, and the user of the information decides how they're going to -- this information is going to be used and presented. This procedure is --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but can I take it then that you don't know whether or not any reports naming the individuals that were collaborating were made to the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know whether any of those individuals that were involved in what was reported to you as collaboration with the KLA were withdrawn from Kosovo by the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, and that was not what we dealt with. Our task was to report on what we had, and then other organs, state organs, those in charge, they resolve matters further and they do not have to report back to us as to whether they had done anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we move on quickly. Have you ever heard of the Joint Command in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What was the Joint Command, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a type of coordinating body. My first information was that it is some coordination, and the information came at the end of June or beginning of July 1998. This information was conveyed to me by General Dimitrijevic, the then-head of the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know what it coordinated?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As General Dimitrijevic said to me then, the then-President Milosevic sent to Kosovo Mr. Sainovic, who was vice-premier of the federal government, and Mr. Minic, who was president of the federal chamber of the Federal Assembly, to coordinate in Kosovo certain political economic activities and to coordinate activities between the Army of Yugoslavia and the MUP in the struggle against terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Apart from Mr. Sainovic and Mr. Minic, do you know who were the members of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I did not know the other members of that body. Later on I found out that there was Mr. Matkovic as well and that Mr. Zoran Andjelkovic joined, too, who was president of the provisional Executive Council and president of the humanitarian organisation of the Red Cross in Kosovo-Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This information you got from Mr. -- From General Dimitrijevic or did you get this later information you speak of from another source?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for these two, I found out later. General Dimitrijevic was not the source.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you know when the Joint Command was terminated?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it ceased to exist towards the end of October, or rather, after the agreement that was achieved between Mr. Holbrooke and Milosevic when the Federal Commission for the implementation of that agreement was established, and Mr. Sainovic was appointed head of that commission. Officially, that's when.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We -- well, do you know of any combat -- or could I show you a document, and perhaps I could ask you to comment on it, P1968. This document has in it an order for the Joint Command of Kosovo dated the 24th of March, 1999 and it's an order to support the MUP in defeating and destroying the terrorist forces in the Drenica sector. Did you know -- well, have you ever seen orders like this before?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It's dated the 24th of March, 1999. Having seen that, do you recall whether or not the Joint Command was still in existence in March 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. At that time I was representative of the administration in the staff of the Supreme Command, and I just know that in the chain of command and according to regulations, there is no Joint Command. And as the Supreme Command Staff, we had no contacts and no communication in writing or orally with a Joint Command. For us there was the command of the 3rd Army and the command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. Can we move on to the Supreme Command, since you mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we look at 3D728, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And I just -- I'm going to ask you to read something and explain to us the meaning of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We have it here. Can we go to page 3 in the English, please, and that's the end of the document in both English and B/C/S, the third -- the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This is one of the briefing notes that you were shown, it's dated the 11th of April, 1999, and it is one that you participated in, according to the front page of it. Can you read the reference at the bottom from where you see: "Colonel-General Ojdanic" and tell us what that is about.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, which section are you referring to towards the bottom? Could you help me with the bullet points, perhaps, the first, second, third one from the bottom or could you give me some guide-line what I should read or should I just give my opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: From the second one from the bottom, and that is where it appears that Colonel-General Ojdanic speaks, that's where you see Colonel-General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's this part here. "During the course of the evening correct directives in relation to ours" -- and then it says: "Attended by present" -- is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what is the date -- what was the date?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is the 11th of April, 1999. It says: "Submit a draft plan for study, the briefing will be at 0900 hours with the Supreme Command," and then it goes on: "Present," and it lists a group of people?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, the original says: "VK," which can be Supreme Command but it can also be a supreme commander as well. The abbreviation in Serbian is VK. It's the very same for both.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You heard that, General. Can you explain just the meaning of this extract?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what this is about. I see that some meeting was envisaged, now was it with the supreme commander, possibly. What the gentleman said just now, both are possible, and also I see who was present. But this is the first time I see this. I really cannot give any comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Doesn't it indicate that present at the meeting at 0900 hours is anticipated to be the chief of the operations administration Lieutenant-General Smiljanic and other persons, is that your understanding of this document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. One can see exactly who was present, probably at some briefing related to a plan, as far as I can see. But what this was, I really do not know. I assume that it is a meeting with the supreme commander, that is to say Milosevic. But if I were to say anything, I'm afraid that I would not be of great assistance to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what this means PPR Sainovic, I don't know what that refers to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp suggested you were present at this briefing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, well maybe if I could remind him -- yes, he was present at the meeting, that is recorded on the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, but I don't remember this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Isn't this -- well, first, isn't this list of persons here the persons who were expected to attend the meeting of the Supreme Command at 0900 hours to study a draft plan? Can you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You see where it says Sainovic, what does it say before that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Sreten, adjutant of the MUP unit from Kosovo. But he's not the adjutant, I don't know. That's how it was translated. Maybe that's how it was translated, the translation is wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who would be translating it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know, but it says here [B/C/S spoken] the adjutant of the MUP unit in Kosovo and that kind of a function did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, these -- it's -- these briefings according to you are prepared by military documents. It is possible that the person taking the record did not know the precise rank of somebody in the MUP. But would you agree with me that having regard to the persons here that the reference -- and when I say the persons, the rank of the person, the reference to Sreten, adjutant for the MUP unit from Kosovo, is a reference to Sreten Lukic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I can agree with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you read what follows? There are two other parts to this after "MUP unit from Kosovo," what does the rest of it say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me, sir, to say it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] PPR stands for vice-president or -- and Colonel-General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So it is -- based on how you read this, this is Vice-President Sainovic and Colonel-General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Supreme Command met how frequently, do you know?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In what period, if you could be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: During the war.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Supreme Command Staff with the Chief of Staff was at the command post and General Ojdanic --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have that information at disposal, that I don't know. But I know that General Ojdanic went to the Commander-in-Chief, President Milosevic, to submit a report on the previous 24-hour period about the activities in that period, and then they'd study this report. And if Milosevic had any remarks to make, any suggestions, any tasks, I know that he would go to see him at a certain time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: During the war in 1998 [sic], and I'm moving on now, who was the member of the Supreme Command responsible for the operation of the military courts? And may I just say I mean the Supreme Command Staff, who was a member of the Supreme Command Staff responsible for the operations of the military courts?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody on the Supreme Command Staff. The military prosecutor's offices and the military courts were under the jurisdiction of the federal minister of defence and the federal defence ministry, and in the General Staff there was a sector, the mobilisation and status issues sector. There was an administration that dealt with legislative issues, control, and so on. So courts were under the jurisdiction of the federal defence ministry. They were under civilian control.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that is the military courts?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. They were under the jurisdiction of the federal ministry. The judges took their oath before the federal defence minister. The General Staff did not have any jurisdiction over military courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you in a position to tell us how many reports about crimes committed by officers during the war in 1998 [sic] were submitted by the VJ to the military courts?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, military courts --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I failed to intervene before, but could we clarify that. For the second time Mr. Stamp is asking a question about the war in 1998. I don't know whether there was any war in 1998 -- I may have missed it, but this may mislead the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before we move back to the question. Mr. Visnjic, can you look at line 9, please, page 89 and the last sentence. Is that what the witness actually said?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I heard the witness say that. That also sounded strange to me, but on the other hand the question that precedes this answer is a bit troublesome. When I look at the question and when I look at the answer, I myself can't tell what is right and what is wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All that matters is that we have a correction reflection of what was said. It can be resolved by other questions later. So let's revert to where we are, Mr. Stamp, and what you're asking is whether -- whether the witness knows the number of reports of -- submitted by the VJ to military courts about crimes committed by officers during --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- The war in 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that at those briefings the chief of the sector that I just mentioned for mobilisation and status issues submitted reports on the reports received from military courts, and I think that at the end the figure stood at between 16 and 18.000 criminal reports that had been filed. And 90 per cent, perhaps even more, related to draft dodging.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, you're saying you think. Who was the chief of the sector?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would be difficult for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Who was the chief of the sector? Who would know?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the sector at that time was the -- was Risto Ratovic, General Risto Ratovic, late general. But the legal administration was part of the part of this sector. It was an expert service. It had no jurisdiction over the military courts, but the military courts would regularly submit reports to this administration about the number of cases with the break-down of the kind of cases and so on, merely to keep them informed..

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
